claim: Human listeners continuously use linguistic context to anticipate upcoming concepts, words, and phonemes during speech processing.
source: It is widely accepted that human listeners continuously use the linguistic context to anticipate upcoming concepts, words, and phonemes.
evidence: This is stated as widely accepted in the field, drawing on established scientific consensus.

claim: Classic psycholinguistic paradigms suggest a two-stage process where acoustic input initially leads to local, context-independent representations, which are then quickly integrated with contextual constraints.
source: Classic psycholinguistic paradigms suggest a two-stage process, in which acoustic input initially leads to local, context-independent representations, which are then quickly integrated with contextual constraints.
evidence: This claim references findings from classic psycholinguistic paradigms, which are cited works in the field.

claim: The brain constructs a single coherent, unified interpretation of input that fully integrates available information across representational hierarchies and uses contextual constraints to modulate even the earliest sensory representations.
source: This contrasts with the view that the brain constructs a single coherent, unified interpretation of the input, which fully integrates available information across representational hierarchies, and thus uses contextual constraints to modulate even the earliest sensory representations.
evidence: This represents an alternative theoretical view in the literature about speech processing.

claim: Listeners employ both local and unified predictive models in parallel during speech perception.
source: Results provide evidence that listeners employ both types of models in parallel.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by MEG data analysis.

claim: Two local context models uniquely predict some part of early neural responses: one based on sublexical phoneme sequences, and one based on phonemes in the current word alone.
source: Two local context models uniquely predict some part of early neural responses, one based on sublexical phoneme sequences, and one based on the phonemes in the current word alone
evidence: This finding is based on the MEG response analysis comparing different context models.

claim: Early responses to phonemes reflect a unified model that incorporates sentence-level constraints to predict upcoming phonemes.
source: at the same time, even early responses to phonemes also reflect a unified model that incorporates sentence-level constraints to predict upcoming phonemes.
evidence: This is a key finding from the MEG data analysis showing sentence-level effects on early phoneme processing.

claim: The anatomical origins of different predictive models are in nonidentical parts of the superior temporal lobes bilaterally.
source: Neural source localization places the anatomical origins of the different predictive models in nonidentical parts of the superior temporal lobes bilaterally
evidence: This is based on MEG source localization analysis.

claim: The right hemisphere shows a relative preference for more local models compared to the left hemisphere.
source: with the right hemisphere showing a relative preference for more local models.
evidence: This lateralization finding is based on comparing predictive power across hemispheres.

claim: Parallel models might make the perceptual system more robust.
source: Parallel models might make the perceptual system more robust
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Parallel models might facilitate processing of unexpected inputs.
source: facilitate processing of unexpected inputs
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Parallel models might serve a function in language acquisition.
source: serve a function in language acquisition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Listeners organize internal representations to minimize the processing cost of future language input.
source: One strategy that listeners employ to achieve this is to organize internal representations in such a way as to minimize the processing cost of future language input (Ferreira and Chantavarin, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ferreira and Chantavarin, 2018.

claim: Listeners actively predict future input using internalized generative models.
source: Different accounts have been proposed for how listeners do this, many centered on the notion that they actively predict future input (Gagnepain et al., 2012), for instance using internalized generative models (Halle and Stevens, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gagnepain et al., 2012 and Halle and Stevens, 1962.

claim: More predictable words are easier to process.
source: Such predictive strategies manifest in a variety of measures that suggest that more predictable words are easier to process (Hale, 2003; Levy, 2008; Smith and Levy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing this effect.

claim: Spoken words are recognized more quickly when heard in a meaningful context.
source: For instance, spoken words are recognized more quickly when they are heard in a meaningful context (Marslen-Wilson and Tyler, 1975)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marslen-Wilson and Tyler, 1975.

claim: Words that are made more likely by context are associated with reduced neural responses compared to less expected words.
source: words that are made more likely by the context are associated with reduced neural responses, compared to less expected words (Holcomb and Neville, 2013; Connolly and Phillips, 1994; Van Petten et al., 1999; Diaz and Swaab, 2007; Broderick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing this neural effect.

claim: Contextual facilitation in speech processing is sensitive to language statistics.
source: This contextual facilitation is pervasive, and is sensitive to language statistics (Willems et al., 2016; Weissbart et al., 2020; Schmitt et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing sensitivity to language statistics.

claim: Contextual facilitation in speech processing is sensitive to discourse level meaning.
source: as well as the discourse level meaning of the language input for the listeners (van Berkum et al., 2003; Nieuwland and Van Berkum, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing sensitivity to discourse meaning.

claim: Phonemes that are inconsistent with known word forms elicit an electrophysiological mismatch response.
source: Phonemes that are thus inconsistent with known word forms elicit an electrophysiological mismatch response (Gagnepain et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gagnepain et al., 2012.

claim: Responses to valid phonemes are proportionately larger the more surprising the phonemes are.
source: responses to valid phonemes are proportionately larger the more surprising the phonemes are (Ettinger et al., 2014; Gwilliams and Marantz, 2015; Gaston and Marantz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing this effect.

claim: Responses to acoustic features in early auditory cortex reflect expectations based on acoustic context.
source: Predictive processing is not restricted to linguistic representations, as even responses to acoustic features in early auditory cortex reflect expectations based on the acoustic context (Singer et al., 2018; Forseth et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singer et al., 2018 and Forseth et al., 2020.

claim: For optimal interpretation of imperfect sensory signals, listeners ought to use the maximum amount of information available to compute a prior expectation for upcoming sensory input.
source: A strong argument for a unified, globally consistent model comes from Bayesian frameworks, which suggest that, for optimal interpretation of imperfect sensory signals, listeners ought to use the maximum amount of information available to them to compute a prior expectation for upcoming sensory input (Jurafsky, 1996; Norris and McQueen, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument from Bayesian frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: Speech processing is truly incremental, with a unified linguistic representation updated at the phoneme time scale.
source: An implication is that speech processing is truly incremental, with a unified linguistic representation that is updated at the phoneme (or an even lower) time scale (Smith and Levy, 2013).
evidence: This is an implication from Bayesian frameworks, supported by a citation to Smith and Levy, 2013.

claim: Recognizing a word can bias subsequent phonetic representations.
source: Such a unified representation is consistent with empirical evidence for top-down modulation of sensory representations, for example, suggesting that recognizing a word can bias subsequent phonetic representations (Luthra et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Luthra et al., 2021.

claim: Listeners weight cues like a Bayes-optimal observer during speech perception.
source: that listeners weight cues like a Bayes-optimal observer during speech perception (Bejjanki et al., 2011; Feldman et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bejjanki et al., 2011 and Feldman et al., 2009.

claim: Listeners immediately interpret incoming speech with regard to communicative goals.
source: and that they immediately interpret incoming speech with regard to communicative goals (Chambers et al., 2004; Heller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2004 and Heller et al., 2016.

claim: During perception of a word, initially multiple meanings are activated regardless of whether they are consistent with sentence context, and contextually appropriate meanings only come to dominate at a later stage.
source: Results from cross-modal semantic priming suggest that, during perception of a word, initially multiple meanings are activated regardless of whether they are consistent with the sentence context or not, and contextually appropriate meanings only come to dominate at a later stage (Swinney, 1979; Zwitserlood, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Swinney, 1979 and Zwitserlood, 1989.

claim: Listeners initially consider word meanings that are impossible given the syntactic context.
source: Similarly, listeners' eye movements suggest that they initially consider word meanings that are impossible given the syntactic context (Gaston et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gaston et al., 2020.

claim: Phoneme sequence probabilities can have effects that are decoupled from the word recognition process.
source: Similarly, at the sublexical level, experiments with nonwords suggest that phoneme sequence probabilities can have effects that are decoupled from the word recognition process (Vitevitch and Luce, 1999; Vitevitch and Luce, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vitevitch and Luce, 1999 and Vitevitch and Luce, 2016.

claim: The two hemispheres differ with respect to their use of context, with the left hemisphere relying heavily on top-down predictions and the right hemisphere processing language in a more bottom-up manner.
source: For example, it has been suggested that the two hemispheres differ with respect to their use of context, with the left hemisphere relying heavily on top-down predictions, and the right hemisphere processing language in a more bottom-up manner (Federmeier, 2007).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by a citation to Federmeier, 2007.

claim: Each context model significantly improves the prediction of held-out MEG data in both hemispheres.
source: Each context model significantly improves predictions of held-out magnetoencephalography (MEG) data in both hemispheres (tmax ≥ 6.16, p ≤ 0.005).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG data analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Surprisal and entropy have similar predictive power in each context model.
source: Surprisal and entropy have similar predictive power in each context model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Table 1 with statistical comparisons.

claim: Cohort- and phoneme entropy at each level significantly improve predictions even when tested individually.
source: Even when tested individually, excluding variability that is shared between the two, cohort- and phoneme entropy at each level significantly improve predictions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with statistical results.

claim: Sentence-constrained phoneme entropy significantly improves predictions, providing evidence for cross-hierarchy integration.
source: A significant effect of sentence-constrained phoneme entropy is evidence for cross-hierarchy integration, as it suggests that sentence-level information is used to predict upcoming phonemes.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The sublexical context model is more right-lateralized than the sentence context model.
source: The sublexical context model is significantly more right-lateralized than the sentence model (t11 = 4.41, p = 0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The word model is numerically but not significantly more right-lateralized than the sentence model.
source: while the word model is only numerically more right-lateralized than the sentence model (t11 = 1.53, p = 0.154).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lateralization indices.

claim: In the right hemisphere, all three context models and the two acoustic models originate from different source configurations.
source: Results indicate that, in the right hemisphere, all three context models, as well as the two acoustic models, originate from different source configurations (F(175, 1925) ≥ 1.25, p ≤ 0.017).
evidence: This is a statistical result from source localization analysis.

claim: In the left hemisphere, the sentence-constrained model is localized differently from all other models.
source: In the left hemisphere, the sentence-constrained model is localized differently from all other models (F(179, 1969) ≥ 1.38, p < 0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from source localization analysis.

claim: There is no significant distinction among the non-sentence models in the left hemisphere.
source: whereas there is no significant distinction among the other models (possibly due to lower power due to the weaker effects in the left hemisphere for all but the sentence model).
evidence: This is a statistical result with a speculative interpretation about power.

claim: The different context models are maintained by at least partially separable neural processes.
source: In sum, these results suggest that the different context models are maintained by at least partially separable neural processes.
evidence: This is an inference from the source localization results.

claim: Responses to surprisal suggest that bottom-up information reaches representations that use sentence- and word-level contexts simultaneously at an early response peak.
source: However, in contrast to this prediction, the observed responses to surprisal suggest that bottom-up information reaches representations that use the sentence- and word-level contexts simultaneously, at an early response peak (Figure 5A; peak in the early time window for sentence context: 78 ms, standard deviation (SD) = 24 ms; word context: 76 ms, SD = 11 ms).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRF peak latencies shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sublexical surprisal is associated with an early peak at 94 ms.
source: Sublexical surprisal is associated with a lower response magnitude overall, but also exhibits an early peak at 94 ms (SD = 26 ms).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRF peak latencies shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The three peak latencies for surprisal responses do not differ significantly.
source: None of these three peak latencies differ significantly (all pairwise t11 ≤ 2.01, p ≥ 0.065).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing peak latencies.

claim: A large, extended response reflecting the sentence context but not the word context starts at around 205 ms.
source: Later in the timecourse the responses dissociate more strongly, with a large, extended response reflecting the sentence context, but not the word context starting at around 205 ms (tmax = 5.27, p = 0.007).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of TRFs shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both cohort representations are associated with an early peak (sentence context: 56 ms; word context: 80 ms).
source: The TRFs to cohort entropy suggest a similar pattern as those to surprisal (Figure 5C, D). Both cohort representations are associated with an early peak (sentence context: 56 ms, SD = 28 ms; word context: 80 ms, SD = 23 ms)
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRF peak latencies shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Only the sentence-constrained cohort shows a later sustained effect following the early peak.
source: followed only in the sentence-constrained cohort by a later sustained effect.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRFs shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Even early responses to cohort entropy are dominated by the sentence context.
source: In contrast to surprisal, however, even early responses to cohort entropy are dominated by the sentence context (tmax = 5.35, p = 0.004 at 43 ms; later responses: tmax = 7.85, p < 0.001 at 461 ms).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing TRFs shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Lexical representations are overall most strongly activated in a model that incorporates the sentence context.
source: This suggests that lexical representations are overall most strongly activated in a model that incorporates the sentence context.
evidence: This is an inference from the cohort entropy results.

claim: Responses to phoneme entropy are similar for all levels of context, dominated by an early and somewhat broader peak.
source: In contrast to surprisal and cohort entropy, the responses to phoneme entropy are similar for all levels of context, dominated by an early and somewhat broader peak (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRFs shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: Early processing is biased toward phoneme entropy while later processing is biased toward cohort entropy.
source: A direct comparison of sentence-constrained cohort and phoneme entropy indicates that early processing is biased toward phoneme entropy (though not significantly) while later processing is biased toward cohort entropy (tmax = 4.74, p = 0.017 at 231 ms).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing different entropy measures.

claim: All context representations drive a predictive model for upcoming phonemes.
source: In sum, the entropy results suggest that all context representations drive a predictive model for upcoming phonemes.
evidence: This is an inference from the phoneme entropy results.

claim: Early activity originates from the vicinity of the auditory cortex in the upper STG, regardless of context.
source: Source localization suggests that early activity originates from the vicinity of the auditory cortex in the upper STG, regardless of context (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on source localization analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The precise source configuration in the right STG differs between contexts in the early time window.
source: The precise source configuration in the right STG nevertheless differs between contexts in the early time window (sentence vs word: F(175, 1925) = 2.08, p < 0.001; word vs sublexical: F(175, 1925) = 5.99, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from source localization analysis.

claim: The sentence-based responses in the midlatency window recruit more sources localized to the middle and inferior temporal lobe.
source: More notably, the sentence-based responses in the midlatency window recruits more sources, localized to the middle and inferior temporal lobe.
evidence: This is based on source localization analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The sentence-based responses in the midlatency window differ significantly from the early window in both hemispheres.
source: Accordingly, the sentence-based responses in the midlatency window differs significantly from the early window (left hemisphere: F(179, 1969) = 1.72, p < 0.001; right hemisphere: F(175, 1925) = 5.48, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from source localization analysis.

claim: Phonetic information initially engages a set of sources in the STG, while a secondary stage engages more ventral sources that specifically represent the sentence context.
source: These results suggest that phonetic information initially engages a set of sources in the STG, while a secondary stage then engages more ventral sources that specifically represent the sentence context.
evidence: This is an inference from the source localization results.

claim: No evidence was found for a trade-off between context models across subjects or across time.
source: No evidence was found for such a trade-off, as correlation between context models were generally neutral or positive across subjects and across time (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Twelve native speakers of English participated in the study (six female, six male, age mean = 21 years, range 19–23).
source: Twelve native speakers of English were recruited from the University of Maryland community (six female, six male, age mean = 21 years, range 19–23).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Eleven participants were right-handed and one was left-handed according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: According to self-report using the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971), 11 were right handed and 1 left handed.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Stimuli consisted of 11 excerpts from the audiobook version of The Botany of Desire by Michael Pollan, totaling 46 minutes and 44 seconds.
source: Stimuli consisted of 11 excerpts from the audiobook version of The Botany of Desire by Michael Pollan (Pollan, 2001). Each excerpt was between 210 and 332 s long, for a total of 46 min and 44 s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Brain responses were recorded with a 157 axial gradiometer whole head MEG system at the University of Maryland, College Park.
source: Brain responses were recorded with a 157 axial gradiometer whole head MEG system (KIT, Kanazawa, Japan) inside a magnetically shielded room (Vacuumschmelze GmbH & Co. KG, Hanau, Germany) at the University of Maryland, College Park.
evidence: This is a description of the data acquisition method.

claim: Excluding the left-handed participant did not change the conclusions from any of the reported lateralization significance tests.
source: While this participant's brain responses were more right-lateralized than average, excluding them did not change the conclusions from any of the reported lateralization significance tests.
evidence: This is a robustness check reported in the results.

claim: The sentence context generally leads to a reduction of word surprisal compared to unigram surprisal.
source: The sentence (5 gram) context generally leads to a reduction of word surprisal, but the magnitude of the reduction differs substantially between words (across all stimuli, mean ± standard deviation, unigram surprisal: 10.76 ± 5.15; 5 gram surprisal: 7.43 ± 5.98; t8172 = 76.63, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sentence-level predictions propagate to phoneme surprisal but not in a linear fashion.
source: Sentence-level predictions propagate to phoneme surprisal, but not in a linear fashion.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2B with examples.

claim: The acoustic features explain more variability in brain responses than the linguistic features.
source: Overall, the acoustic features explain more of the variability in brain responses than the linguistic features (compare scales in Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is based on comparing predictive power shown in Figure 4.

claim: Speech is an acoustically rich stimulus, driving many kinds of auditory receptive fields.
source: This is likely because speech is an acoustically rich stimulus, driving many kinds of auditory receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference to explain why acoustic features have high predictive power.

claim: The linguistic predictors represent very specific computations, likely represented in a small and specialized neural territory.
source: In contrast, the linguistic predictors represent very specific computations, likely represented in a small and specialized neural territory.
evidence: This is an inference to explain why linguistic features have lower predictive power than acoustic features.

claim: The linguistic modulation of brain responses can be detected very reliably across subjects.
source: For the present purpose, what is critical is the consistency of the linguistic effects across subjects: Figure 4B,C, as well as the effect sized shown in Table 1 suggests that the linguistic modulation of brain responses can be detected very reliably across subjects.
evidence: This is based on the consistency of effects shown in Figure 4B, C and Table 1.

claim: The significant predictive power of the local context models is inconsistent with the hypothesis of a single, unified context model.
source: The significant predictive power of the local context models is inconsistent with the hypothesis of a single, unified context model (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference from the data results compared to the theoretical model.

claim: Different neural representations incorporate different kinds of context.
source: Instead, it suggests that different neural representations incorporate different kinds of context.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that local context models have predictive power.

claim: Phoneme and cohort entropy were highly correlated (sentence context: r = 0.92; word context: r = 0.90).
source: Even though phoneme and cohort entropy were highly correlated (sentence context: r = 0.92; word context: r = 0.90)
evidence: This is a statistical result describing the correlation between predictors.

claim: Each of the four entropy representations was able to explain unique variability in the MEG responses that could not be attributed to any of the other representations.
source: each of the four representations was able to explain unique variability in the MEG responses that could not be attributed to any of the other representations (Figure 4C, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: The sentence context model is not restricted to predicting upcoming words, but also generates expectations for upcoming phonemes.
source: This suggests that the sentence context model is not restricted to predicting upcoming words, but also generates expectations for upcoming phonemes.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that sentence-constrained phoneme entropy explains unique variance.

claim: The brain maintains a unified context model but also maintains more local context models.
source: Together, these results thus indicate that the brain does maintain a unified context model, but that it also maintains more local context models.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesizing the results.

claim: The predictive power of the joint linguistic model (predictors from all three levels combined) is not significantly lateralized.
source: however, the predictive power of the joint linguistic model (predictors from all three levels combined) is not significantly lateralized (tmax = 4.11, p = 0.134).
evidence: This is a statistical result from lateralization analysis.

claim: Linguistic processing is bilateral, but the hemispheres differ in what context models they rely on.
source: These results thus suggest that linguistic processing is bilateral, but that the hemispheres differ in what context models they rely on.
evidence: This is an inference from the lateralization results.

claim: The left hemisphere primarily relies on a unified model of the sentence context, and the right hemisphere more broadly keeps track of different context levels.
source: These lateralization patterns suggest an anatomical differentiation in the representations of different context models, with the left hemisphere primarily relying on a unified model of the sentence context, and the right hemisphere more broadly keeping track of different context levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the lateralization patterns observed.

claim: Multiple predictive models process speech input in parallel.
source: Together, these results suggest that multiple predictive models process speech input in parallel.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the results.

claim: Three different neural systems receive the speech input in parallel, each updated incrementally by arriving phonemes but differing in the extent and kind of context incorporated.
source: An architecture consistent with these observations is sketched in Figure 8: three different neural systems receive the speech input in parallel. Each representation is updated incrementally by arriving phonemes. However, the three systems differ in the extent and kind of context that they incorporate, each generating its own probabilistic beliefs about the current word and/or future phonemes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the results, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The unified model has the most explanatory power and clearly bilateral representation among the linguistic models.
source: Among the linguistic models, the unified model has the most explanatory power and clearly bilateral representation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The unified model was associated with extended activation for up to 600 ms and recruitment of more ventral regions of the temporal lobe.
source: In addition, while activity in local models was short lived, the unified model was associated with extended activation for up to 600 ms and recruitment of more ventral regions of the temporal lobe (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the TRF analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The update in the unified model is normally more extensive than the local models.
source: This suggests that the update in the unified model is normally more extensive than the local models
evidence: This is an inference from the extended activation pattern.

claim: The unified model most commonly drives semantic as well as form representations, while the short-lived local models might be restricted to form-based representations.
source: and could indicate that the unified model most commonly drives semantic as well as form representations, while the short-lived local models might be restricted to form-based representations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the activation patterns.

claim: Parallel activation of lexical candidates based on sentence and word context models can explain short-lived priming of sentence-inappropriate candidates.
source: Parallel activation of lexical candidates based on sentence and word context models can explain these findings. Short-lived brain responses (up to 150 ms after phoneme onset) show evidence of parallel activation of sentence-constrained as well as sentence-independent word candidates. The coexistence of these two candidate sets can explain short-lived priming of sentence-inappropriate candidates.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current results to previous findings in the literature.

claim: Brain responses related to sentence-appropriate candidates exhibit a secondary, sustained response (150–550 ms), explaining selective priming of sentence-appropriate candidates at longer delays.
source: Whereas brain responses related to sentence-independent candidates are transient, brain responses related to sentence-appropriate candidates exhibit a secondary, sustained response (150–550 ms), explaining selective priming of sentence-appropriate candidates at longer delays.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current results to previous findings in the literature.

claim: Maintaining alternative, sentence-independent candidates or sublexical probabilistic phoneme sequences might enable faster recovery when sentence-based predictions turn out to be misleading.
source: If context-constrained candidates are immediately available, then why maintain alternative, sentence-independent candidates or even sublexical probabilistic phoneme sequences? One functional advantage might be faster recovery when sentence-based predictions turn out to be misleading.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the parallel models.

claim: Contextually unexpected continuations in reading are not associated with a proportional increase in processing cost.
source: Such an effect has been described in reading, where contextually unexpected continuations are not associated with a proportional increase in processing cost (Frisson et al., 2017; Luke and Christianson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frisson et al., 2017 and Luke and Christianson, 2016.

claim: A representation of sublexical phoneme sequences might be functionally relevant when encountering input that is noisy or not yet part of the lexicon.
source: Similarly, a representation of sublexical phoneme sequences might be functionally relevant when encountering input that is noisy or not yet part of the lexicon.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation.

claim: Phoneme transition probabilities are generally higher within words than between words, such that low probability phoneme transitions are cues to word boundaries.
source: Phoneme transition probabilities are generally higher within words than between words, such that low probability phoneme transitions are cues to word boundaries (Cairns et al., 1997; Harris, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cairns et al., 1997 and Harris, 1955.

claim: Statistical phoneme sequence models might play an important role in language acquisition by bootstrapping lexical segmentation of continuous speech.
source: Statistical phoneme sequence models might thus play an important role in language acquisition by bootstrapping lexical segmentation of continuous speech (Cairns et al., 1997; Chambers et al., 2003; Saffran et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: In adult speech perception, phoneme sequence models might have a function when encountering novel words, such as domain-specific vocabularies or personal names.
source: Even in adult speech perception, they might have a similar function when encountering novel words, such as domain-specific vocabularies or personal names (Norris and McQueen, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The linguistic context can be highly informative for phoneme recognition.
source: Finally, the linguistic context can be highly informative for phoneme recognition (Hitczenko et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hitczenko et al., 2020.

claim: Different levels of context might make complementary contributions to phoneme recognition.
source: and different levels of context might make complementary contributions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: The different models might play more differentiated roles in different listening conditions, such as unpredictable conversations or speech in noise.
source: It is conceivable that the different models play more differentiated roles in different listening conditions, for example in unpredictable conversations or speech in noise.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future research.

claim: Multiple probabilistic cohort representations seem to be maintained in parallel.
source: Perhaps the most surprising implication of our results is that multiple probabilistic cohort representations seem to be maintained in parallel.
evidence: This is an inference from the results.

claim: Two different cohort entropy predictors both explain unique variability in the data, one based on lexical frequency and another based on contextual likelihood.
source: This is most directly implied by the result that two different cohort entropy predictors both explain unique variability in the data, one based on the lexical frequency of each candidate, and another based on the contextual likelihood of each candidate.
evidence: This is based on the statistical results from the MEG analysis.

claim: The finding of multiple cohort representations is inconsistent with models in which each lexical candidate is assigned a single 'activation' value.
source: This is inconsistent with models in which each lexical candidate is assigned a single 'activation' value (e.g., Morton, 1969).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the results to existing models, with a citation.

claim: The results might be reconciled with models that distinguish between a lexical item's entry in long-term memory and its instantiation as a token for parsing a speech signal.
source: It might be more readily reconciled with models that distinguish between a lexical item's entry in long-term memory, and its instantiation as a token for parsing a speech signal, since such a mechanism allows for multiple tokens corresponding to the same lexical item (McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris, 1994; Norris and McQueen, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to relevant models.

claim: Existing models generally are restricted to a single 'arena' for lexical competition, whereas the current results imply the possibility that competition plays out in parallel in at least partially different brain systems.
source: Yet, existing models generally are restricted to a single 'arena' for lexical competition, whereas our results imply the possibility that the competition plays out in parallel in at least partially different brain systems.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the results to existing models.

claim: The observed phoneme entropy effects indicate that phoneme-level expectations are modulated by the sentence context.
source: A second implication is that feedback from the sentence-level context can and does affect phoneme processing. The observed phoneme entropy effects indicate that phoneme-level expectations are modulated by the sentence context.
evidence: This is an inference from the phoneme entropy results.

claim: The finding of sentence-level modulation of phoneme expectations is inconsistent with models that assume a pure bottom-up process of word recognition.
source: This is inconsistent with some models of word recognition that assume a pure bottom-up process (e.g., Norris et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the results to existing models, with a citation.

claim: In multistage architectures that allow different priors at sequential hierarchical levels, higher levels receive the posterior interpretation of the input from lower levels rather than the unbiased input itself.
source: In multistage architectures that allow different priors at sequential hierarchical levels (such as Figure 1B), higher levels receive the posterior interpretation of the input from the lower levels, rather than the unbiased input itself.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about sequential architectures.

claim: In sequential architectures, the prior of lower-level systems is allowed to distort the bottom-up evidence before it is compared to the prior generated by higher levels, which is suboptimal from a Bayesian perspective.
source: This is suboptimal when considering a Bayesian model of perception, because the prior of lower-level systems is allowed to distort the bottom-up evidence before it is compared to the prior generated by higher levels (Norris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument with a citation.

claim: The parallel model allows undistorted bottom-up information to be directly compared with the context model for each definition of context.
source: In contrast, the parallel representations favored by the evidence presented here allow undistorted bottom-up information to be directly compared with the context model for each definition of context.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical advantage of the parallel model.

claim: The parallel model can accommodate empirical evidence for feedback while avoiding the theoretical problem associated with sequential models.
source: The parallel model can thus accommodate empirical evidence for feedback while avoiding this theoretical problem associated with sequential models.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical advantage of the parallel model.

claim: Previous research showing an early influence of sentence context on speech processing has typically relied on specifically designed, highly constraining contexts which are highly predictive of a specific lexical item.
source: Previous research showing an early influence of sentence context on speech processing has typically relied on specifically designed, highly constraining contexts which are highly predictive of a specific lexical item (Holcomb and Neville, 2013; Connolly and Phillips, 1994; Van Petten et al., 1999; Rommers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research with citations.

claim: In highly predictive contexts, listeners might predict specific items, and such predictions might be linked to the left-lateralized speech production system.
source: In such highly predictive contexts, listeners might indeed predict specific items, and such predictions might be linked to the left-lateralized speech productions system (Federmeier, 2007; Pickering and Gambi, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations.

claim: Specific item prediction would be less useful in more representative language samples where highly predictable words are rare.
source: However, such a mechanism would be less useful in more representative language samples, in which highly predictable words are rare (Luke and Christianson, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference with a citation.

claim: In situations of limited predictability, reading time data suggest that readers make graded predictions over a large number of possible continuations.
source: In such situations of limited predictability, reading time data suggest that readers instead make graded predictions, over a large number of possible continuations (Luke and Christianson, 2016; Smith and Levy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reading time studies.

claim: What looks like graded predictions could actually be preactivation of specific higher-level semantic and syntactic features shared among likely items.
source: Alternatively, it has also been suggested that what looks like graded predictions could actually be preactivation of specific higher-level semantic and syntactic features shared among the likely items (Altmann and Kamide, 1999; Luke and Christianson, 2016; Matchin et al., 2019; Pickering and Gambi, 2018; Van Berkum et al., 2005), without involving prediction of form-based representations.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis from the literature with citations.

claim: The present results provide evidence in favor of graded probabilistic and form-based predictions at least down to the phoneme level.
source: The present results, showing brain responses reflecting sentence-constrained cohort- and phoneme entropy, provide a new kind of evidence in favor of graded probabilistic and form-based predictions at least down to the phoneme level.
evidence: This is an inference from the current results.

claim: Lexical/phonetic processing is largely bilateral.
source: Our results suggest that lexical/phonetic processing is largely bilateral.
evidence: This is an inference from the lateralization results.

claim: The bilateral nature of lexical/phonetic processing is consistent with extensive clinical evidence for bilateral receptive language ability.
source: This is consistent with extensive clinical evidence for bilateral receptive language ability (Gazzaniga and Sperry, 1967; Kutas et al., 1988; Poeppel, 2001; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The right hemisphere might play a distinct role in complex, real-world language processing.
source: and suggestions that the right hemisphere might even play a distinct role in complex, real-world language processing (Federmeier et al., 2008; Jung-Beeman, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Results from visual half-field reading studies suggest that lexical processing in both hemispheres is dominated by sentence meaning.
source: Overwhelmingly, results from these studies suggest that lexical processing in both hemispheres is dominated by sentence meaning (Coulson et al., 2005; Federmeier et al., 2005; Federmeier and Kutas, 1999; Wlotko and Federmeier, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to visual half-field studies.

claim: The strong bilateral representation of the unified model of speech found in the current study is consistent with visual half-field reading studies.
source: This is consistent with the strong bilateral representation of the unified model of speech found here.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current results to previous findings.

claim: The similarity of response latencies in the two hemispheres implies that right-hemispheric effects are unlikely to be due to interhemispheric transfer from the left hemisphere.
source: As in the visual studies, the similarity of the response latencies in the two hemispheres implies that right-hemispheric effects are unlikely to be due to interhemispheric transfer from the left hemisphere (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the latency results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Visual half-field reading studies have indicated a pattern suggesting that the left hemisphere processes language in a maximally context-sensitive manner, whereas the right hemisphere processes sensory input in a bottom-up manner, unbiased by linguistic context.
source: Visual half-field reading studies have indicated a pattern of hemispheric differences, which has been interpreted as indicating that the left hemisphere processes language in a maximally context-sensitive manner, whereas the right hemisphere processes the sensory input in a bottom-up manner, unbiased by the linguistic context (Federmeier, 2007).
evidence: This is a characterization of previous findings with a citation.

claim: The current results suggest a modification of the proposal that the right hemisphere processes language in a bottom-up manner, indicating that both hemispheres rely on sentence-based, graded predictions, but that the right hemisphere additionally maintains stronger representations of local contexts.
source: Our results suggest a modification of this proposal, indicating that both hemispheres rely on sentence-based, graded predictions, but that the right hemisphere additionally maintains stronger representations of local contexts.
evidence: This is an inference from the current results compared to previous proposals.

claim: Lateralization might depend on task characteristics such as stimulus familiarity.
source: Finally, lateralization might also depend on task characteristics such as stimulus familiarity (Brodbeck et al., 2018a)
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with a citation.

claim: In highly constraining contexts the left hemisphere might engage the left-lateralized language production system to make specific predictions.
source: and in highly constraining contexts the left hemisphere might engage the left-lateralized language production system to make specific predictions (Federmeier, 2007; Pickering and Gambi, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with citations.

claim: The sentence context was approximated with a 5-gram model that provides an accurate estimate of the sum of local constraints based on a context of the four preceding words only.
source: We approximated the sentence context with a 5 gram model. This model provides an accurate estimate of the sum of local constraints, based on a context of the four preceding words only.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: The 5-gram model misses the more subtle influences of the larger context, both semantic constraints and syntactic long-range dependencies.
source: However, it misses the more subtle influences of the larger context, both semantic constraints and syntactic long-range dependencies, which might make the sentence level even more different from the local context models.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the model.

claim: Lexical N-gram models conflate the influence of syntactic, semantic, and associative constraints.
source: Furthermore, lexical N gram models conflate the influence of syntactic, semantic, and associative constraints (e.g., idioms).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the model.

claim: Work with more sophisticated language models can reveal an even more complex relationship between global and local contexts.
source: It is thus possible that work with more sophisticated language models can reveal an even more complex relationship between global and local contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future research.

claim: Robust speech processing is based on probabilistic predictions using different context models in parallel, cutting across hierarchical levels of representations.
source: Here, we show that this assumption might have been misleading, because different predictive models are maintained in parallel. Our results suggest that robust speech processing is based on probabilistic predictions using different context models in parallel, and cutting across hierarchical levels of representations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
